result:
The Rain Keeps a Ledger

There is a particular shade of gray that only exists in cities just after rainfall—when the asphalt becomes a mirror and the streetlights blur into watercolor. I was standing under a broken awning yesterday, watching people hurry past with their collars up, each one carrying an entire universe behind their eyes.

We talk about crowds as if they are one thing, a single organism flowing through the veins of concrete. But a crowd is never singular. It is thousands of parallel novels being written in real time, each page turning with every heartbeat. The woman with the green umbrella might be rehearsing a goodbye she hasn’t said yet. The old man feeding pigeons could be remembering a garden that no longer exists. The child in yellow boots is probably inventing a language that only she understands.

I think about this often: that consciousness is the most private experience in the world, and yet we share it. We are all protagonists to ourselves and background characters to everyone else, and somehow that asymmetry doesn’t break us. It binds us. We move through each other’s stories like ghosts—brief, weightless, but real.

There is a kind of ethics in this, I believe. If you truly understand that every stranger is living a life as vivid and complicated as your own, cruelty becomes not just wrong but absurd. How could you diminish a story you haven’t read? How could you close a book you haven’t opened?

The rain stopped. The city exhaled. And for a moment, under that broken awning, I felt the strange, tender gravity of being here—small, temporary, and impossibly connected.
